content:
The image shows a plant stem at or near the soil line with the following key features:

- **White, cottony/fluffy mycelial growth** on the stem surface near the soil line
- **Dark, irregular sclerotia** (hardened fungal bodies) embedded within or adjacent to the white mycelium — these appear as small, dark, rounded structures
- The stem tissue beneath is rotted and bleached/pale in color
- The lesion is located at the crown/base of the stem, right at the soil interface
- Upper plant tissue appears wilted/dead (dry, tan foliage visible above)

**Reasoning:**

- The white cottony mycelium combined with **visible sclerotia** (hard, dark survival bodies) at the stem base is the hallmark of **Southern Blight** (*Sclerotium rolfsii*). Sclerotia in Southern Blight are typically small, round, and mustard-seed to pea-sized, often appearing white when young and tan/brown when mature — consistent with what is visible here.
- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot** (*Sclerotinia sclerotiorum*) also produces white mycelium and sclerotia, but its sclerotia are larger and elongated/irregular, and the disease typically affects upper stem tissue more.
- **Southern Bacterial Wilt** would not produce visible white mycelium or sclerotia.
- The crown/soil-line location, white mycelium, and small round sclerotia all strongly point to Southern Blight.
